abstract.title: ABSTRACT
abstract.p: Trastuzumab Rezetecan (SHR‐A1811) is an antibody‐drug conjugate (ADC) targeting the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2). It features a novel enzyme‐cleavable linker and delivers the topoisomerase I inhibitor payload, rezetecan, with a drug‐to‐antibody ratio of approximately 6.0. Its population pharmacokinetics (PopPK) were characterized using a nonlinear mixed‐effects model based on data from 645 patients with HER2‐expressing or HER2‐mutated advanced solid tumors with 18,671 samples across three phase 1 trials. A two‐analyte PopPK model was developed to describe the intact ADC and released payload. The intact ADC followed a two‐compartment model with linear elimination, while the payload rezetecan was best described by a one‐compartment model with first‐order release and linear elimination. Stepwise covariate modeling identified several baseline factors—body weight, tumor size, albumin, aspartate aminotransferase, age, and cancer type—as statistically significant parameters‐covariates' relationships. However, their effects on the AUC of both intact ADC and payload were limited (< 20% change). No clinically relevant impacts were observed for race, sex, formulation, or renal/hepatic function on ADC or payload exposure. In conclusion, the developed PopPK model adequately characterizes the pharmacokinetics of Trastuzumab Rezetecan and its released payload. Based on the covariate analysis, no dose adjustments are warranted for the studied patient population. This model can further support dose selection in future clinical trials through exposure–response analyses.

list-item.p:
What is the current knowledge on the topic? ○
Trastuzumab Rezetecan, a novel antibody‐drug conjugate (ADC) targeting the human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2). It features a novel enzyme‐cleavable linker and delivers the topoisomerase I inhibitor payload, rezetecan, with a drug‐to‐antibody ratio of approximately 6.0. It has promising efficacy across different indications (such as NSCLC, BC, and CRC) and a tolerable safety profile observed from several clinical trials.

What question did this study address? ○
This is the first published analysis for the PK characteristics of the intact ADC, Trastuzumab rezetecan, and the released payload rezetecan. This analysis assessed potential covariates that may significantly impact the PK parameters and derived exposures.

What does this study add to our knowledge? ○
This study describes the combined population pharmacokinetics model for Trastuzumab rezetecan and its released payload rezetecan, and the results of the covariates' assessment. No dose adjustment based on the retained covariates is warranted.

How might this change drug discovery, development, and/or therapeutics? ○
This model, together with exposure‐response analysis, is being used to support the dose selection of Trastuzumab Rezetecan in several indications.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) is a member of the human epidermal growth factor receptor family, which also includes HER1 or EGFR, HER3, and HER4 [1, 2, 3, 4]. The HER2 gene has shown gene amplification/overexpression in more than 30% of all human cancers, including breast cancer, non‐small cell lung cancer, ovarian cancer, gastric cancer, gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma, and colorectal cancer [5]. The current standard first‐line treatment for HER2‐positive unresectable or metastatic breast cancer involves a combination of HER2‐targeted monoclonal antibodies trastuzumab and Pertuzumab administered alongside a taxane chemotherapy. Following disease progression, the antibody–drug conjugate (ADC) trastuzumab emtansine is generally recommended as second‐line therapy [6, 7, 8].

Trastuzumab rezetecan (SHR‐A1811) is a HER2‐targeting ADC developed by Jiangsu Hengrui Pharmaceuticals Co. Ltd. Trastuzumab rezetecan is composed of anti‐HER2 antibody trastuzumab, a cleavable linker, and the topoisomerase I inhibitor payload rezetecan. The payload rezetecan demonstrates higher membrane permeability and more potent cell‐killing efficacy compared to the payload of Trastuzumab Deruxtecan (T‐Dxd) [9]. To enhance chemical stability, a chiral cyclopropyl group has been introduced between the linker and toxin, preventing uncontrolled toxin release and reducing early release–related side effects. The minimal amount of early‐released payload contributes to a favorable safety profile of Trastuzumab rezetecan [10]. Trastuzumab rezetecan can specifically bind to the HER2 on the tumor cell surface, and subsequently the conjugate is endocytosed into the cell, prior to endocytosis of the conjugate and transport into the lysosome. The free toxin rezetecan, which inhibits the activity of DNA topoisomerase I, is released via cathepsin hydrolysis and leads to tumor cell apoptosis [11]. Rezetecan has a bystander killing effect, due to high permeability that allows penetration into the surrounding cancer cells after release from HER2+ tumor cells and subsequent killing of those surrounding cells, including HER2‐negative cancer cells [11].

Trastuzumab rezetecan has recently received conditional approval from the China National Medical Products Administration (NMPA) for marketing in May 2025 [11]. It is indicated for the treatment of adult patients with unresectable locally advanced or metastatic non‐small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) harboring HER2‐activating mutations who have previously received at least one systemic therapy [12]. As the third‐generation HER2‐ADC, Trastuzumab rezetecan is currently undergoing multiple clinical trials for indications including HER2+ breast cancer, HER2‐low breast cancer, HER2‐expressing advanced gastric cancer, gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) adenocarcinoma and colorectal cancer, and HER2‐expressing advanced gynecological cancer [13, 14].

The objectives of this analysis were first to build and qualify a population pharmacokinetics (PopPK) model of intact Trastuzumab rezetecan and its released payload in patients with HER2‐expressing or mutated advanced solid tumors. Moreover, such PopPK modeling allows evaluating potential PK differences between different cancer types and liver and kidney functions, as well as assessing the interindividual variability (IIV) and identifying covariates that may explain part of this variability.

sec.title: Analysis Dataset
sec.p: Trastuzumab rezetecan was administered every 3 weeks (dose range, 1.0–8.0 mg/kg) with a treatment cycle length of 21 days. This design was the pattern in data from three phase I studies in advanced solid tumor patients: SHR‐A1811‐I‐101 (HER2‐expressing or mutated advanced solid tumors), SHR‐A1811‐I‐102 (HER2‐expressing advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma and colorectal cancer), and SHR‐A1811‐I‐103 (advanced NSCLC who have HER2 expression, amplification, or mutation). These studies were approved by the relevant ethics committee and were carried out in accordance with the International Conference on Harmonization (ICH) Good Clinical Practice guidelines (ICH, 2016) and the Declaration of Helsinki (World Medical Association, 2013). Details regarding the study populations, dosing regimens, and pharmacokinetic (PK) sampling schedules are summarized in Table S1.

Serum concentrations of intact ADC were determined by a validated electrochemiluminescence assay, with lower limit of quantification (LLOQ) of 1.00 μg/mL. Concentrations of the released payload were measured via liquid chromatography–tandem mass spectrometry with an LLOQ of 0.05 ng/mL. Patients who received at least one Trastuzumab rezetecan dose and had at least one measurable PK sample of intact ADC or released payload were included in the analysis. In total, the final analysis data set included 18,671 samples from 645 patients.

sec.title: Software
sec.p: Population PK modeling for intact Trastuzumab rezetecan and released payload was performed using the first‐order conditional estimation with interaction (FOCE‐I) method in NONMEM (version 7.5.1) (ICON Development Solutions, Ellicott City, MD). Model diagnostics and some exploratory plots, including covariate testing, were conducted by Xpose and Perl‐Speaks‐NONMEM (PsN) (version 4.6.0) (Uppsala University, Uppsala, Sweden). Data exploration, postprocessing of NONMEM outputs, and simulation activities were carried out using R (version 4.1.2).

sec.title: Population Pharmacokinetic Modeling Approach
sec.p: A sequential two‐step approach was used in this analysis. First, the PK profiles of intact ADC were fitted to the model. Then PK parameter estimates, including both fixed‐ and random‐effects terms of the intact ADC, were fixed, and only the parameters of released payload were estimated. The one‐step approach was also considered, and the estimated model parameters, model stability and run duration from both approaches were compared. For the base model characterization, a systematic evaluation of model structures was conducted, including the payload formation process, payload elimination pathways (linear or nonlinear). The IIV of all PK parameters was described by an exponential model. Moreover, residual variability (RUV) relationships assessed included additive, proportional, and combined (additive and proportional) error terms for both the intact ADC and payload.

The assessed covariates were based on prior knowledge of the intact ADC Trastuzumab rezetecan and the released payload rezetecan. Correlations between covariates were first explored to identify confounding factors. Correlations between post hoc individual random effects and covariates were then explored using pairwise correlations. Covariates were screened using a stepwise approach, which included forward inclusion followed by backward deletion. During the forward inclusion, covariates that resulted in a reduction in objective function value (OFV) by more than 6.63 (χ2, p value ≤ 0.01, df = 1) were retained. During the backward deletion, covariates were removed one by one from the full model. The covariates that resulted in an increase in OFV by less than 10.8 (χ2, p value ≤ 0.001, df = 1), as compared to the previous step, were respectively used for the selection of covariates in the final model.

Model selection was based on statistical criteria such as the change in the log‐likelihood function, goodness of fit plots, precision of parameter estimates, (η‐ and σ‐) shrinkage, and scientific and physiological plausibility.

The predictive performance of the models was assessed based on prediction‐corrected visual predictive checks (VPC) [15] performed on major steps of model building, including the base and final models. Evaluation of model robustness and parameter precision was conducted using the nonparametric bootstrap. A total of at least 200 replicated data sets were generated and then fitted to the model to obtain the parameter estimate and 95% confidence interval (CI).

sec.title: Model‐Based Simulations and Applications
sec.p: The impact of the retained parameter‐covariate relationships on the exposures of intact trastuzumab rezetecan and released payload at steady state, that is, area under the concentration‐time curve (AUCss), peak concentration (C max,ss), and trough concentration (C min,ss), was examined in both univariate and multivariate approaches. For the univariate approach, simulations were performed by varying each covariate value one at a time and keeping other covariates as constant (i.e., categorical covariates were set at the reference categories and continuous covariate values were set to the median values in the data set). Exposures of intact ADC and released payload at the 5th and 95th percentiles of the continuous covariates, or at each level of the categorical covariates, were then compared with the exposure estimates for a reference patient (with typical covariate values) via a forest plot. A total of 1000 simulations were conducted for each covariate effect.

For the multivariate approach, individual intact ADC and released payload exposures were estimated from the empirical Bayesian estimates (EBEs), and then summarized and compared among retained covariates or subgroups of interest, such as race, formulation, sex, age, cancer type, hepatic function categories [16], and renal function categories [17]. Specifically, individual EBEs from NSCLC patients included in the final model for intact trastuzumab rezetecan and payload were used to simulate the corresponding individual concentration‐time profiles with the 4.8 mg/kg every‐3‐weeks dosing regimen [18].

sec.title: Population Pharmacokinetic Analysis Datasets
sec.p: The PopPK dataset from 645 patients provided 26,988 records, including 8317 dosing records and 18,671 concentration records (9421 for ADC, 9250 for released drug). The PK profiles stratified by study and dose level are presented in Figure 1 for both intact ADC and released payload, respectively. Intact Trastuzumab rezetecan concentration profiles follow a biphasic pattern, suggesting a two‐compartment model. The PK profiles of the released payload appear to be driven by the intact Trastuzumab rezetecan elimination kinetics. Descriptive statistics of subject categorical and continuous covariates for the population PK datasets are presented in Tables S2 and S3, respectively.

caption.p: The mean pharmacokinetic profiles by study and dose derived from rich sampling after the first administration for the intact ADC (left panels—A, C and E) and released payload (right panels—B, D and F). Colored lines in figures indicate different ADC doses.

sec.title: Development of Intact Trastuzumab Rezetecan Model
sec.p: The intact Trastuzumab rezetecan PK profiles were well‐described by a two‐compartment model with first‐order absorption and elimination. A schematic of the model structure is shown in Figure 2. The IIV was estimated on all parameters and was assumed to have a lognormal distribution. The residual variability was best explained by a combined proportional and additive error. The typical value of the clearance (CL), central volume of distribution (V1), inter‐compartment clearance (Q), and peripheral volume of distribution (V2) of intact Trastuzumab rezetecan were 0.360 L/day, 2.86 L, 0.162 L/day, and 2.88 L, respectively. The covariate effects in the model showed intact Trastuzumab rezetecan CL increasing with increasing body weight (BW) and baseline target lesion diameter (SOD_B). The V1 was increasing with increased body weight and age, and the V2 and V1 were decreasing with increasing baseline albumin (ALB). Equations for CL and V1/V2 are listed below.

caption.p: The population pharmacokinetic model structure of the intact ADC. CL, intact ADC clearance; Q, inter‐compartment clearance; and V1 and V2 for central and peripheral volume of intact ADC, respectively. CL3, released payload clearance; V3, released payload volume of distribution; Krel, release‐rate constant, Krel = RAT during Cycle 1 and Krel = RAT * ALPHA after Cycle 1.

sec.p: The final population PK parameters and bootstrap results for the final model are presented in Table 1. The relative standard error (RSE) for the PK parameters ranged from < 1% to 31.6%, indicating good precision of model parameter estimates. The IIV was 8.7%, 23.5%, 33.6%, and 8.90% for CL, V1, Q, and V2, respectively, and the shrinkage ranged from 6.20% to 56.0%. Parameter estimates of the final intact ADC model were in good agreement with the bootstrap results (included within the 95% CI). The goodness‐of‐fit diagnostics (Figure 3A) and VPC (Figure 4A) confirmed the good predictive performance of the PopPK model.

sec.title: Released‐Toxin Rezetecan Model
sec.p: The PopPK model for the payload Rezetecan formation was dependent on the ADC elimination. The released payload PK was described by a one‐compartment model, with first‐order release rate from the intact ADC, as a fraction of the ADC clearance, and a first‐order elimination (Figure 2). The time course of intact trastuzumab rezetecan concentrations, adjusted for the molar mass, was the input to the released‐payload model. Released payload concentrations tended to decrease after treatment Cycle 1. Therefore, different release‐rate constants (Krel) were considered for Cycle 1 and the following cycles, as previously reported for other ADCs [19]. Time‐varying release‐rate constant (Krel), depending on time or on treatment cycles, was also evaluated, but it did not improve the model fit. Based on an evaluation of various options, Krel was estimated to be equal to RAT with a fixed shift (ALPHA) toward a reduction in Krel after cycle 1, as follows:

The formation of the payload via a different route, such as deconjugation (independent of the intact ADC clearance), was also explored either in lieu or on top of the previously described one. However, this exploration resulted in unstable and/or overparameterized model (i.e., high condition number). The volume of distribution of the released payload (V3) was fixed at 30 L, similar to previously reported value of exatecan mesylate, to avoid identifiability issues [19, 20]. IIV was evaluated on all PK parameters, including release‐rate of released payload from intact Trastuzumab rezetecan (RAT), the ratio of release rate after cycle 1 as compared to cycle 1 (ALPHA), and the clearance of released‐toxin rezetecan (CL3), were 0.814 day−1, 0.693, and 392 L/day, respectively. Following the same covariate assessment procedures as described for the intact ADC, the following parameter‐covariate relationships were found to be statistically significant and were included in the final model for released toxin:

The final released payload PopPK model parameters are presented in Table 1, along with results from the corresponding bootstrap analysis. Parameter estimates were precise, with relative standard errors (RSE) ranging from 1.35% to 51.6%, and shrinkage values between 19.7% and 44.3%. All parameter estimates fell within the 95% confidence intervals of the bootstrap results. The model demonstrated good overall fit, with most of the concentrations well captured. Although a slight underprediction was observed at higher payload concentrations, the goodness‐of‐fit diagnostics (Figure 3B) and visual predictive checks (VPC, Figure 4B) support the good predictive performance of the final PopPK model.

A different modeling strategy was explored in parallel with the aim of a one‐step approach. To do so, once the base model of the intact ADC was built, the base model of the released payload was added, while unfixing the model parameters of the ADC, prior to covariates' assessment. This resulted in parameters' estimates close to the final two‐step PopPK model. This suggests the absence of any bias related to the two‐step approach. However, the run duration was about 6‐fold as compared to the two‐step model, thus significantly increasing the time needed for covariate assessment and bootstrap. In addition, the diagnostic plots for the payload still suggested a tendency to underpredict the higher payload concentrations. The two‐step approach was kept to proceed with the covariate assessment and final PopPK model selection.

sec.title: Influence of Covariates on Intact Trastuzumab Rezetecan Exposures
sec.p: Forest plots of the impact of covariates on steady‐state exposures (AUCss, C max,ss, and C min,ss) in the final model are shown in Figure 5A–C, respectively. Higher body weight levels with the 95th percentile of 82 kg led to a 16.8% increase in AUCss compared to a typical patient. A reduction of 14.2% in AUCss was predicted in patients of lower body weight levels with the 5th percentile of 45 kg. Baseline target lesion diameter (SOD_B) with the 95th and 5th percentiles, 149 mm and 15 mm, also had a slight impact on exposure < 15% compared to a typical patient. Baseline age (AGE) and baseline albumin (ALB) had minor impacts on exposures (< 10%). All covariates were within the non‐clinically meaningful range of 80%–125% of the point estimate of the covariates. Comparisons of steady‐state exposures of intact trastuzumab rezetecan with the 4.8 mg/kg every‐3‐weeks dosing regimen and stratified by hepatic and renal function categories (HFC and RFC, respectively), formulation, sex, age (≥ 65 and < 65), cancer type (CT) and ethnicity (RACE) are presented in Figures S1–S7. There is no remarkable difference in predicted exposures of Trastuzumab rezetecan between ethnicity groups or hepatic or renal function categories.

caption.p: Forest plot of covariate effects on intact Trastuzumab Rezetecan exposure. The solid vertical line corresponds to a ratio of 1 and represents the typical patient. Points and whiskers represent the ratio and 90% CI, respectively. A typical patient is defined as a 56‐year‐old with body weight 60.6 kg, ALB 42.5 g/L, and SOD 52 mm.

sec.title: Influence of Covariates on Released Payload Exposures
sec.p: Following the same approach, forest plot illustrating relative changes in released payload steady‐state exposures (AUCss, C max,ss, and C min,ss) when covariates were varied one at a time are presented in Figure 6A–C, respectively. The 5th and 95th covariate values had < 20% impact as compared to the median. The steady‐state exposure of released payload with the 4.8‐mg/kg every‐3‐weeks dosing regimen was similar when patients were stratified by hepatic and renal function categories (HFC and RFC, respectively), formulation, sex, age (≥ 65 and < 65), cancer type (CT) and ethnicity (RACE).

caption.p: Forest plot of covariate effects on released payload rezetecan exposures. The solid vertical line corresponds to a ratio of 1 and represents the typical patient. Points and whiskers represent the ratio and 90% CI, respectively. A typical patient is defined as a 56‐year‐old NSCLC patient with body weight 60.6 kg, SOD 52 mm, and AST 25 U/L.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Trastuzumab Rezetecan is a novel ADC recently approved by the NMPA for patients with HER2‐mutant, unresectable, locally advanced or metastatic NSCLC harboring HER2 activating mutations who have previously received at least one prior systemic therapy. This analysis represents the first characterization of the PopPK profiles of Trastuzumab rezetecan and released payload, including data from 645 patients enrolled in three clinical trials involving HER2‐positive, unresectable and/or metastatic breast cancer and other solid tumors. The released payload exhibited formation‐limited kinetics; nonetheless, the released payload is not anticipated to influence the PK of the intact Trastuzumab Rezetecan. We have shown that the PK of intact Trastuzumab Rezetecan is adequately described by a two‐compartment model with linear elimination. The exposure (C max and AUC) of intact Trastuzumab Rezetecan increased proportionally over the dose range of 1.0–8.0 mg/kg. A trend toward nonlinear elimination was, however, observed at the lower doses of 1.0 and 2.0 mg/kg, suggesting potential target‐mediated drug disposition (TMDD) at these dose levels. This is a common pattern for monoclonal antibodies exhibiting TMDD and was previously reported for Trastuzumab Rezetecan. During the base model development, several elimination structures were evaluated, including linear, nonlinear, and parallel linear and nonlinear elimination. However, due to the limited data available from the lower‐dose groups (six patients each in the 1.0 and 2.0 mg/kg cohorts), incorporating a nonlinear elimination component did not significantly improve model performance. Moreover, these lower doses are considered suboptimal for efficacy and are unlikely to be included in the current dosing regimen, even though more data would have supported the characterization of the TMDD model parameterization. Moreover, the nonlinear elimination pathway accounted for approximately 5% of total elimination across the observed concentration range. Therefore, a model with linear clearance only was ultimately selected for Trastuzumab Rezetecan.

The pharmacokinetics of the released payload were driven by the intact Trastuzumab Rezetecan clearance, with its profile showing an initial increase and reaching peak concentrations within 2–12 h after dosing. During the base model development, structural models with both constant and time‐varying release rates were evaluated. The model assuming a constant release rate resulted in largely biased predictions and a significantly higher objective function value (OFV) compared to the selected released payload base model. Consequently, distinct release‐rate constants (Krel) for Cycle 1 and subsequent cycles were incorporated. The decrease in release rate after cycle 1 may be influenced by multiple mechanisms. As Trastuzumab Rezetecan contains a linker designed for selective cleavage within tumor cells [21], tumor shrinkage over time could influence drug release and clearance. A semi‐mechanistic model linking time‐varying Krel to tumor shrinkage was initially tested but proved infeasible, likely due to limited longitudinal tumor‐size data. Therefore, empirical models were therefore investigated and found to adequately describe the observed concentration‐time profiles of the released drug. Similar empirical approaches have been used for other ADCs, such as brentuximab vedotin, where released drug formation was modeled to decline exponentially over time, reflecting ADC proteolysis and deconjugation [22]. Further evaluation may be warranted once additional data from ongoing clinical studies become available. Although there is some trend for underprediction of the highest payload concentrations, the model overall provides an acceptable fit to the data, even though any subsequent analyses (such as exposure‐response) considering the payload C max values should be interpreted with caution.

Body weight, albumin, tumor size, and age were identified as statistically significant covariates influencing the pharmacokinetics of intact Trastuzumab Rezetecan. Clearance of Trastuzumab Rezetecan increased with higher body weight, which is consistent with known monoclonal antibody behavior [23]. Given that dosing is weight‐based, higher body weight results in a higher administered dose, leading to a net effect of slightly increased exposure. Compared to a typical patient, steady‐state AUC decreased by 14.2% at the 5th percentile of body weight (45 kg) and increased by 16.8% at the 95th percentile (82 kg). Body weight, age, AST, and cancer type were also significant covariates for the released payload. However, as with the intact ADC, these factors did not show a clinically meaningful impact on steady‐state exposure, and no dose adjustment is warranted. Elevated AST levels were associated with an 18.1% increase in AUCss at the 95th percentile of AST values.

Although the conversion rate from ADC to released drug varied among cancer types, the resulting differences in payload exposure remained within 20%. There were differences between the breast and gastric cancer patient populations in average body weight and sex ratio, which may account for the difference in exposure. In addition, the majority (60%) of patients included in this data set were patients with breast cancer; therefore, further assessment may be needed with additional data from patients with other tumor types. Studies evaluating the safety and efficacy of trastuzumab rezetecan in patients with HER2‐expressing advanced gastric or gastroesophageal junction adenocarcinoma, HER2‐positive or HER2‐mutated unresectable and/or metastatic non‐small cell lung cancer [24], and HER2‐expressing advanced colorectal cancer are also currently ongoing [9], which may provide further insight into its pharmacokinetics across these tumor types. The covariate assessment indicated that the retained covariates had only minor effects on exposure (< 10% change). Post hoc comparisons confirmed comparable exposure levels of both intact ADC and released payload across subgroups defined by race, sex, formulation, and hepatic or renal function.
